claims.text: Preservation of local atomic structure and chemical state governs the high-temperature structural and chemical stability of multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles.
Temperature-controlled in-situ XAS can probe the local atomic structure and chemical state of these nanoparticles during high-temperature operation.
The relevant initial materials include multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles spanning different compositions and structures.
Coordination numbers, bond lengths, and oxidation states represent the proposed local structural and chemical mediator.
Local atomic structure and chemical state influence nanoparticle structural and chemical stability.
Structural and chemical stability affects catalytic and thermoelectric performance.
Nanoparticles that preserve their local atomic structure and chemical state will have improved structural and chemical stability.
Improved structural and chemical stability will enhance catalytic and thermoelectric performance.
The proposed baseline comprises either nanoparticles not characterized by in-situ XAS or nanoparticles with compromised local atomic structure and chemical state.
The hypothesis applies when noble-metal content is below an unspecified threshold.
Lack of correlation between local structure or chemical state and stability would falsify the hypothesis.
Lack of an effect of stability on catalytic or thermoelectric performance would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The conditions include thermoelectric operation from 473 K, but the stated boundary begins at 773 K, leaving the 473–772 K portion of the proposed service regime inconsistently excluded.

In-situ XAS is presented as a characterization probe rather than a material-modifying intervention, yet absence of XAS characterization is used as a baseline alongside compromised material structure. Characterization status is therefore conflated with the physical state proposed to cause stability.
